1690	generality, it is common to work with $\Pic_{(X/S)\fppf}$ and call it
  1691	{\it the\/} Picard functor.
  1692	  \end{rmk}
  1693	
  1694	\section{Relative effective divisors}\label{sc:red}
  1695	
  1696	Grothendieck constructed the Picard scheme by taking a suitable family
  1697	of effective divisors and forming the quotient modulo linear
  1698	equivalence.  This section develops the basic theory of these notions.
  1699	
  1700	\begin{sbs}[Effective divisors] \label{sb:ediv}
  1701	 A closed subscheme $D\subset X$ is called an {\it effective (Cartier)
  1702	divisor\/} if its ideal $\mc I$ is invertible.  Given an $\mc
  1703	O_{\!X}$-module $\mc F$ and   $n\in\bb Z$, set
  1704		$$\mc F(nD):=\mc F\ox\mc I^{\ox -n}.$$
  1705	
  1706	In particular, $\mc O_{\!X}(-D)=\mc I$.  So the inclusion $\mc I\into\mc
  1707	O_{\!X}$ yields, via tensor product with $\mc O_{\!X}(D)$, an injection
  1708	$\mc O_{\!X}\into \mc O_{\!X}(D)$, which, in turn, corresponds to a
  1709	global section of $\mc O_{\!X}(D)$.  This section is not arbitrary since
  1710	it corresponds to an injection.  Sections corresponding to injections
  1711	are termed {\it regular}.
  1712	
  1713	Conversely, given an arbitrary invertible sheaf $\mc L$ on $X$, let
  1714	$\uH^0(X,\mc L)_{\reg}$ denote the subset of $\uH^0(X,\mc L)$ consisting
  1715	of the regular sections, those corresponding to injections $\mc
  1716	L^{-1}\into\mc O_{\!X}$.  And let $|\mc L|$ denote the set of effective
  1717	divisors $D$ such that $\mc O_{\!X}(D)$ is, in some way, isomorphic to $\mc
  1718	L$.  For historical reasons, $|\mc L|$ is called the {\it complete
  1719	linear system\/} associated to $\mc L$ (but $|\mc L|$ needn't be a $\I P^n$ 
  1720	if $X$ isn't integral).
  1721	 \end{sbs}
  1722	
  1723	\begin{ex}\label{ex:lsys}
  1724	 Under the conditions of (\ref{sb:ediv}), establish a canonical isomorphism
  1725	     $$\uH^0(X,\mc L)_{\reg}\big/\uH^0(X,\mc O_{\!X}^*)\risom|\mc L|.$$
  1726	  \end{ex}
  1727	
  1728	\begin{dfn}\label{df:red}
  1729	 A {\it relative effective divisor\/} on $X/S$ is an effective divisor
  1730	$D\subset X$ that is  $S$-flat.
  1731	 \end{dfn}
  1732	
  1733	\begin{lem}\label{lm:ctn}
  1734	 Let $D\subset X$ be a closed subscheme, $x\in D$ a point, and $s\in S$
  1735	its image.  Then the following statements are equivalent:
  1736	 \begin{enumerate}
  1737	  \item The subscheme $D\subset X$ is a relative effective divisor at
  1738	$x$ (that is, in a neighborhood of $x$).
  1739	  \item The schemes $X$ and $D$ are $S$-flat at $x$, and the fiber $D_s$
  1740	is an effective divisor on $X_s$ at $x$. 
  1741	  \item The scheme $X$ is $S$-flat at $x$, and the subscheme $D\subset
  1742	X$ is cut out at $x$ by one element that is regular (a nonzerodivisor)
  1743	on the fiber $X_s$.
  1744	 \end{enumerate}
  1745	\end{lem}
  1746	
  1747	\begin{proof} 
  1748	 For convenience, set $A:=\mc O_{S,s}$ and denote its residue field by
  1749	$k$.  In addition, set $B:=\mc O_{\!X,x}$ and $C:=\mc O_{D,x}$.  Then
  1750	$B\ox_A k=\mc O_{\!X_s,x}$.
  1751	
  1752	Assume (i), and let's prove (ii).  By hypothesis, $D$ is an effective
  1753	divisor at $x$.  So there is a regular element $b\in B$ that generates
  1754	the ideal of $D$.  Multiplication by $b$ defines a short exact sequence
  1755		$$0\to B\to B\to C\to0.$$
  1756	 In turn, this sequence induces the following exact sequence:
  1757	 $$\Tor^A_1(B,k)\to\Tor^A_1(B,k)\to\Tor^A_1(C,k)\to B\ox k\to B\ox k.$$
  1758	
  1759	By hypothesis, $D$ is $S$-flat at $x$; hence, $\Tor^A_1(C,k)=0$.  So
  1760	$B\ox k\to B\ox k$ is injective.  Its image is the ideal of $D_s$.  Thus
  1761	$D_s$ is an effective divisor.
  1762	
  1763	Since $\Tor^A_1(C,k)=0$, the map $\Tor^A_1(B,k)\to\Tor^A_1(B,k)$ is
  1764	surjective.  This map is given by multiplication by $b$, and $b$ lies in
  1765	the maximal ideal of $B$.  Also, $\Tor^A_1(B,k)$ is a finitely
  1766	generated $B$-module.  Hence,  $\Tor^A_1(B,k)=0$ by Nakayama's lemma.
  1767	Therefore, by the local criterion of flatness \cite[Thm.~5.6,
  1768	p.~98]{SGA1} or \cite[Thm.~6.1, p.~73]{OB72}, $B$ is $A$-flat; in other
  1769	words, $X$ is $S$-flat at $x$.  Thus (ii) holds.
  1770	
  1771	Assume (ii).  To prove (iii), denote the ideal of $D$ in $B$ by $I$, and
  1772	that of $D_s$ in $B\ox k$ by $I'$.  Take an element $b\in I$ whose image $b'$ 
  1773	in $B\ox k$ generates $I'$; such a $b$ exists because $D_s$ is an
  1774	effective divisor at $x$ by hypothesis.  For the same reason, $b'$ is
  1775	regular.  It remains to prove $b$ generates $I$. 
  1776	
  1777	Consider the short exact sequence
  1778	%% \begin{equation}\label{eq:3a}
  1779		$$0\to I\to B\to C\to0.$$
  1780	%%  \end{equation}
  1781	 By hypothesis, $C$ is $A$-flat.  Hence the map $I\ox k\to B\ox k$ is
  1782	injective.  Its image is $I'$, which is generated by $b'$.  So the image
  1783	of $b$ in $I\ox k$ generates it.  Hence, by Nakayama's lemma, $b$
  1784	generates $I$.  Thus (iii) holds.
  1785	 
  1786	Assume (iii).  To prove (i), again denote the ideal of $D$ in $B$ by
  1787	$I$.  By hypothesis, $I$ is generated by an element $b$ whose image $b'$
  1788	in $B\ox k$ is regular.  We have to prove $b$ is regular and $C$ is
  1789	$A$-flat.
  1790	
  1791	The exact sequence $0\to I\to B\to C\to0$ yields this one:
  1792	 \begin{equation}\label{eq:3a}
  1793	  \Tor^A_1(B,k)\to\Tor^A_1(C,k)\to I\ox k\to B\ox k.
  1794	  \end{equation}
  1795	 The last map is injective for the following reason.  Since $I=Bb$,
  1796	multiplication by $b$ induces a surjection $B\to I$, so a surjection
  1797	$B\ox k\to I\ox k$.  Consider the composition
  1798		$$B\ox k\to I\ox k\to B\ox k.$$
  1799	 It is given by multiplication by $b'$, so is injective because $b'$ is
  1800	regular. Hence $B\ox k\risom I\ox k$.  Therefore, $I\ox k\to B\ox k$ is
  1801	injective.
  1802	
  1803	By hypothesis, $B$ is $A$-flat.  So $\Tor^A_1(B,k)=0.$ Hence the
  1804	exactness of (\ref{eq:3a}) implies $\Tor^A_1(C,k)=0$.  Therefore, by the
  1805	local criterion, $C$ is $A$-flat.
  1806	
  1807	Since $B$ and $C$ are $A$-flat and $0\to I\to B\to C\to0$ is exact, also
  1808	$I$ is $A$-flat.
  1809	
  1810	Define $K$ by the exact sequence  $0\to K\to B\to I\to0$.  Then the
  1811	sequence
  1812		$$0\to K\ox k\to B\ox k\to I\ox k\to0$$
  1813	 is exact since $I$ is $A$-flat.  But $B\ox k\risom I\ox k$. Hence $K\ox
  1814	k=0$.  Therefore, $K=0$ by Nakayama's lemma.  But $K$ is the kernel of
  1815	multiplication by $b$ on $B$.  So $b$ is regular.  Thus (i) holds.
  1816	 \end{proof}
  1817	
  1818	\begin{ex}\label{ex:sum}
  1819	 Let $D$ and $E$ be relative effective divisors on $X/S$, and $D+E$
  1820	their sum. Show $D+E$ is a relative effective divisor too.
  1821	 \end{ex}
  1822	
  1823	\begin{dfn}\label{df:div}
  1824	 Define a functor $\Div_{X/S}$ by the formula
  1825	    $$\Div_{X/S}(T):=\{\,\text{relative effective divisors $D$
  1826	     on $X_T/T$}\,\}.$$
  1827	 \end{dfn}
  1828	
  1829	Note $\Div_{X/S}$ is indeed a functor.  Namely, given a relative
  1830	effective divisor $D$ on $X_T/T$ and an arbitrary $S$-map $p\:T'\to T$,
  1831	we have to see the $T'$-flat closed subscheme $D_{T'}\subset
  1832	X_{T'}$ is an effective divisor.  So let $\mc I$ denote the ideal of
  1833	$D$.  Since $D$ is $T$-flat, $p_{X_T}^*\mc I$ is equal to the ideal of
  1834	$D_{T'}$.  But, since $\mc I$ is invertible, so is $p_{X_T}^*\mc I$.
  1835	Thus $D_{T'}$ is a (relative) effective divisor.
  1836	
  1837	\begin{thm}\label{th:repDiv}
  1838	 Assume $X/S$ is projective and flat.  Then $\Div_{X/S}$ is
  1839	representable by an open subscheme $\IDiv_{X/S}$ of the Hilbert scheme
  1840	$\IHilb_{X/S}$.
  1841	 \end{thm}
  1842	
  1843	\begin{proof}
  1844	 Set $H:=\IHilb_{X/S}$, and let $W\subset X\x H$ be the universal
  1845	(closed) subscheme, and $q\:W\to H$ the projection.  Let $V$ denote the
  1846	set of points $w\in W$ at which $W$ is an effective divisor. Plainly $V$
  1847	is open in $W$.  Set $Z:=q(W-V)$.  Then $Z$ is closed because $q$ is
  1848	proper.  Set $U:=H-Z$.  Then $U$ is open, and $q^{-1}U$ is an effective
  1849	divisor in $X\x U$.  In fact, since $q$ is flat, $q^{-1}U$ is a relative
  1850	effective divisor in $X\x U/U$.
  1851	
  1852	It remains to show that $U$ represents $\Div_{X/S}$.  So let $T$ be an
  1853	$S$-scheme, and $D\subset X_T/T$ a relative effective divisor.  By the
  1854	universal property of the pair $(H,W)$, there exists a unique map
  1855	$g\:T\to H$ such that $g_X^{-1}W=D$.  We have to show that $g$ factors
  1856	through $U$.
  1857	
  1858	For each $t\in T$, the fiber $D_t$ is an effective divisor since it is
  1859	obtained by base change (or owing to Lemma~\ref{lm:ctn}).  But
  1860	$D_t=W_{g(t)}\ox k_t$ where $k_t$ is the residue field of $t$.  So
  1861	$W_{g(t)}$ too is a divisor, as a field extension is faithfully flat.
  1862	Hence, since $X\x H$ and $W$ are $H$-flat, $W$ is, by
  1863	Lemma~\ref{lm:ctn}, a relative effective divisor along the fiber over
  1864	$g(t)$.  Therefore, $g(t)\in U$.  So, since $U$ is open, $g$ factors
  1865	through $U$.
  1866	 \end{proof}
  1867	
  1868	\begin{ex}\label{ex:DivC}
  1869	  Assume $f\:X\to S$ is flat and is projective Zariski locally over $S$.
  1870	Assume its fibers are curves, that is, of {\it pure} dimension 1.  Given
  1871	$m\ge1$, let $\Div_{X/S}^m$ be the functor whose $T$-points are the
  1872	relative effective divisors $D$ on $X_T/T$ with fibers $D_t$ of degree
  1873	$m$.
  1874	
  1875	Show the $\Div_{X/S}^m$ are representable by open and closed subschemes
  1876	of finite type $\IDiv_{X/S}^m\subset\IDiv_{X/S}$, which are disjoint and
  1877	cover.
  1878	
  1879	Let $X_0\subset X$ be the subscheme where $X/S$ is smooth.  Show
  1880	$X_0=\IDiv_{X/S}^1$.
  1881	
  1882	Let  $X_0^m$ be the $m$-fold  $S$-fibered product.  Show there is a natural
  1883	$S$-map $$\alpha\:X_0^m\to\IDiv_{X/S}^m,$$ which is given on  $T$-points
  1884	by $\alpha(\Gamma_1,\dotsc,\Gamma_m)= \sum \Gamma_i$.
  1885	 \end{ex}
  1886	
  1887	\begin{rmk}\label{rmk:symprod}
  1888	 Consider the map $\alpha$ of Exercise~\ref{ex:DivC}.  Plainly $\alpha$
  1889	is compatible with permuting the factors of $X_0^m$.  Hence $\alpha$
  1890	factors through the symmetric product $X_0^{(m)}$.  In fact, $\alpha$
  1891	induces an isomorphism
  1892		$$X_0^{(m)}\risom \IDiv_{X_0/S}^m.$$
  1893	 This isomorphism is treated in detail in \cite[Prp.~6.3.9,
  1894	p.~437]{De73} and in outline in \cite[Prp.~3, p.~254]{BLR}.
  1895	 \end{rmk}
  1896	
  1897	\begin{sbs}[The module $\mc Q$]\label{sb:Q}
  1898	 Assume $f\:X\to S$ is proper, and let $\mc F$ be a coherent $\mc
  1899	O_{\!X}$-module flat over $S$.  Recall from \cite[7.7.6]{EGAIII2} that there
  1900	exist a coherent $\mc O_{\!S}$-module $\mc Q$ and an isomorphism of functors
  1901	in the quasi-coherent $\mc O_{\!S}$-module $\mc N$:
  1902	 \begin{equation}\label{eq:Q}
  1903		q\:\SHom(\mc Q, \mc N)\risom f_*(\mc F\ox f^*\mc N).
  1904	 \end{equation}
  1905	  The pair $(\mc Q, q)$ is unique, up to unique isomorphism, and by
  1906	\cite[7.7.9]{EGAIII2}, forming it commutes with changing the base, in
  1907	particular, with localizing.
  1908	
  1909	Fix $s\in S$ and assume $S=\Spec(\mc O_{S,s})$.  Note that the following
  1910	conditions are equivalent:
  1911	 \begin{enumerate}
  1912	  \item the $\mc O_{\!S}$-module $\mc Q$ is free (or equivalently,
  1913	projective);
  1914	  \item the functor $\mc N\mapsto f_*(\mc F\ox f^*\mc N)$ is right
  1915	exact;
  1916	  \item for all $\mc N$, the natural map is an isomorphism, $f_*(\mc
  1917	F)\ox \mc N\risom f_*(\mc F\ox f^*\mc N)$;
  1918	  \item the natural map is a surjection,
  1919	 $\uH^0(X,\mc F)\ox k_s\onto\uH^0(X_s,\mc F_s)$.
  1920	 \end{enumerate}
  1921	 Indeed, the equivalence of (i)--(iii) is elementary and straightforward.
  1922	Moreover, (iv) is a special case of (iii).  Conversely, (iv) implies
  1923	(iii) by \cite[7.7.10]{EGAIII2} or \cite[Cor.~5.1 p.~72]{OB72}; this
  1924	useful implication is known as the ``property of exchange.''
  1925	
  1926	In addition, (i)--(iv) are implied by the following condition:
  1927	 \begin{enumerate}\setcounter{enumi}{4}
  1928	  \item the first cohomology group of the fiber vanishes, $\uH^1(X_s,\mc
  1929	F_s)=0$.
  1930	 \end{enumerate} 
  1931	 Indeed, (v) implies that $\tu R^1f_*(\mc F\ox f^*\mc N)=0$ for all $\mc
  1932	N$ by \cite[7.5.3]{EGAIII2} or \cite[Cor.~2.1 p.~68]{OB72}; in turn, this
  1933	vanishing implies (ii) owing to the long exact sequence of higher direct
  1934	images.
  1935	 \end{sbs}
  1936	
  1937	\begin{ex}\label{ex:gc&r}
  1938	%%   Assume $f\:X\to S$ is proper and flat.  Assume its geometric
  1939	  Assume $f\:X\to S$ is proper and flat, and its geometric fibers are
  1940	reduced and connected.  Show $\mc O_{\!S}\risom f_*\mc O_{\!X}$ holds
  1941	universally.
  1942	 \end{ex}
  1943	
  1944	\begin{dfn}\label{df:LinSys}
  1945	Let $\mc L$ be an invertible sheaf on $X$.  Define a subfunctor
  1946	$\LinSys_{\mc L/X/S}$ of $\Div_{X/S}$ by the formula
  1947	  \begin{multline*}
  1948	   \LinSys_{\mc L/X/S}(T):=\{\,\text{relative effective divisors $D$
  1949	     on $X_T/T$ such that}\\
  1950	     \text{$\mc O_{\!X_T}(D)\simeq \mc L_T\ox f_T^*\mc N$
  1951	%%      \text{$\mc O_{\!X_T}(D)\simeq(\mc L|X_T)\ox f_T^*\mc N$
  1952			for some invertible sheaf $\mc N$ on }T\,\}.
  1953	  \end{multline*}
  1954	 \end{dfn}
  1955	
  1956	Notice the similarity of this definition with that,
  1957	Definition~\ref{df:Pfs}, of $\Pic_{X/S}$: both definitions work with
  1958	isomorphism classes of invertible sheaves on $X_T$ modulo $\Pic(T)$, in
  1959	the hope of producing a representable functor.  Here, this hope is
  1960	fulfilled under suitable hypotheses on $f$, according to the next
  1961	theorem.
  1962	
  1963	\begin{thm}\label{th:LinSys} Assume $X/S$ is proper and flat, and its
  1964	geometric fibers are integral.  Let $\mc L$ be an invertible sheaf on
  1965	$X$, and let $\mc Q$ be the $\mc O_{\!S}$-module associated in
  1966	Subsection~\ref{sb:Q} to $\mc F:=\mc L$. Set $L:=\I P(\mc Q)$.  Then $L$
  1967	represents $\LinSys_{\mc L/X/S}$.
  1968	 \end{thm}
  1969	
  1970	\begin{proof}
  1971	 Let $D\in\LinSys_{\mc L/X/S}(T)$.  Say $\mc O_{\!X_T}(D)\simeq \mc
  1972	L_T\ox f_T^*\mc N$.  Then $\mc N$ is determined up to isomorphism.
  1973	Indeed, let $\mc N'$ be a second choice.  Then $$\mc L_T\ox f_T^*\mc
  1974	N\simeq\mc L_T\ox f_T^*\mc N'.$$  So $f_T^*\mc N\simeq f_T^*\mc N'$
  1975	since $\mc L$ is invertible.  Hence $\mc N\simeq\mc N'$ by
  1976	Lemma~\ref{lm:fff}, which applies to $f_T\:X_T\to T$ since $\mc
  1977	O_{\!S}\risom f_*\mc O_{\!X}$ holds universally by Exercise~\ref{ex:gc&r}.
  1978	
  1979	Say $D$ is defined by $\sigma\in\uH^0(X_T,\mc L_T\ox f_T^*\mc N)$.
  1980	Now, forming $\mc Q$ commutes with changing the base to $T$, and so
  1981	(\ref{eq:Q}) becomes
  1982	 \begin{equation}\label{eq:QT}
  1983	  \SHom(\mc Q_T, \mc N)\risom f_{\smash{T}*}(\mc L_T\ox f_T^*\mc N).
  1984	 \end{equation}
  1985	 Hence $\sigma$ corresponds to a map $u\:\mc Q_T\to\mc N$.
  1986	 
  1987	Let $t\in T$.  Since $D$ is a relative effective divisor on $X_T/T$, its
  1988	fiber $D_t$ is a divisor on $X_t$ by Lemma~\ref{lm:ctn}.  Since $D_t$ is
  1989	defined by $\sigma_t\in \uH^0(X_t,\mc L|X_t)$, necessarily $\sigma_t
  1990	\neq 0$.  But $\sigma_t$ corresponds to $u\ox k_t$, so $u\ox k_t\neq 0$.
  1991	Now, $\mc N$ is invertible, so $\mc N\ox k_t$ is a $k_t$-vector space of
  1992	dimension 1.  So $u\ox k_t$ is surjective.  Hence, by Nakayama's lemma,
  1993	$u$ is surjective at $t$.  But $t$ is arbitrary.  So $u$ is surjective
  1994	everywhere.
  1995	
  1996	Therefore, $u\:\mc Q_T\to\mc N$ defines an $S$-map $p\:T\to L$ by
  1997	\cite[4.2.3]{EGAII}.  Since $(\mc N, u)$ is determined up to
  1998	isomorphism, a second choice yields the same $p$.
  1999	
  2000	Plainly, this construction is functorial in $T$.  Thus we obtain a map
  2001	of functors,
  2002	\begin{equation*}
  2003	 	\Lambda\:\LinSys_{\mc L/X/S}(T)\to L(T).
  2004	 \end{equation*}
  2005	 Let us prove  $\Lambda$  is an isomorphism.
  2006	
  2007	Let $p\in L(T)$, so  $p\:T\to L$ is an $S$-map.  Then $p$  arises from a
  2008	%% Consider an $S$-map $p\:T\to L$.  It arises from a
  2009	surjection $u\:\mc Q_T\onto\mc N$; namely, $u=p^*\alpha$ where
  2010	$\alpha\:\mc Q_L \onto\mc O(1)$ is the tautological map.  Moreover,
  2011	there is only one such pair $(\mc N, u)$ up to isomorphism.
  2012	
  2013	Via the isomorphism in (\ref{eq:QT}), the surjection $u$

  2043	\section{The Picard scheme}\label{sc:Psch}
  2044	
  2045	This section proves Grothendieck's main theorem about the Picard scheme,
  2046	which asserts its existence if $X/S$ is projective and flat and its
  2047	geometric fibers are integral; in fact, the functor $\Pic_{(X/S)\et}$ is
  2048	representable.  The proof involves Grothendieck's method of using
  2049	functors to prescribe patching.  The basic theory is developed in
  2050	\cite[Ch.~0, Sct.~4.5, pp.~102--107]{EGAG}, and is applied in
  2051	\cite[Ch.~1, Sct.~9, pp.~354--401]{EGAG} to the construction of
  2052	Grassmannians and related parameter schemes.  The present construction
  2053	involves the basic theory, but is more sophisticated and more
  2054	complicated because it works not simply with the Zariski topology, but
  2055	also with the \'etale topology.

  2057	\begin{dfn}\label{df:Psch}

  2059	is representable, then the representing scheme is called the {\it Picard
  2060	scheme\/} and denoted by $\IPic_{X/S}$.  Moreover, we say simply that the
  2061	Picard scheme $\IPic_{X/S}$ exists.
  2062	 \end{dfn}

  2065	at most one Picard scheme.  Of course, if any functor is representable,
  2066	then the representing scheme is uniquely determined, up to a unique
  2067	isomorphism that preserves the identification of the given functor
  2068	with the functor of points of the representing scheme.  But here, there
  2069	is more to the story.

  2072	$\IPic_{X/S}$.  Then, by descent theory, $\Pic_{(X/S)\et}$ is already a
  2073	sheaf in the fppf topology; so it is equal to its associated sheaf
  2074	$\Pic_{(X/S)\fppf}$.  Hence, it too is representable by $\IPic_{X/S}$.
  2075	On the other hand, $\Pic_{X/S}$ may or may not be representable;
  2076	however, if it is, then it, as well, must be representable by $\IPic_{X/S}$.

  1266	\section{The several Picard functors}\label{sc:Pfctrs}
  1267	\renewcommand{\theequation}{\thethm.\arabic{equation}}
  1268	Our first job is to identify a likely candidate for the functor of
  1269	points of the Picard scheme.  In fact, there are several reasonable such
  1270	Picard functors, and each one is more likely to be representable than
  1271	the preceding.  In this section, they all are formally introduced and
  1272	compared.
  1273	
  1274	\begin{dfn}\label{df:aPf}
  1275	 The {\it absolute Picard functor} $\Pic_X$ is the functor from  the
  1276	 category of (locally Noetherian) $S$-schemes $T$ to the category of
  1277	abelian groups defined by the formula
  1278		$$\Pic_X(T):=\Pic(X_T).$$
  1279	\end{dfn}
  1280	
  1281	The absolute Picard functor  is a ``prepared presheaf'' in this
  1282	sense: given any family of  $S$-schemes $T_i$, we have
  1283		$$\Pic_X\bigl(\textstyle\coprod T_i\bigr)=\prod\Pic_X(T_i).$$
  1284	 Hence, given a covering family $\{T_i\to T\}$ in the Zariski topology,
  1285	the \'etale topology, or any other Grothendieck topology on the category
  1286	of $S$-schemes, there is no harm, when we consider the sheaf associated
  1287	to $\Pic_X$, in working simply with the single map $T'\to T$ where
  1288	$T':=\coprod T_i$.  And doing so lightens the notation, making for
  1289	easier reading. Therefore, we do so throughout, calling $T'\to T$ simply
  1290	a {\it covering\/} in the given topology.
  1291	
  1292	The absolute Picard functor $\Pic_X$ is never a separated presheaf in
  1293	the Zariski topology.  Indeed, take an $S$-scheme $T$ that carries an
  1294	invertible sheaf $\mc N$ such that $f^*_T\mc N$ is nontrivial.  (For
  1295	example, take $T:=\I P^1_X$ and $\mc N:=\mc O_{\!T}(1)$.  Then the diagonal
  1296	map $X\to X\x X$ induces a section $g$ of $f_T$; that is, $gf_T=1_T$.
  1297	Hence $f^*_T\mc N$ is nontrivial.)  Now, there exists a Zariski covering
  1298	$T'\to T$ such that the pullback $\mc N|T'$ is trivial; here, $T'$ is
  1299	simply the disjoint union of the subsets in a suitable ordinary open
  1300	covering of $T$.  So the pullback $f^*_{T'}\mc N|X_{T'}$ is trivial too.
  1301	Thus $\Pic_X(T)$ has a nonzero element whose restriction is zero in
  1302	$\Pic_X(T')$.
  1303	
  1304	According to descent theory, every representable functor is a sheaf in
  1305	the Zariski topology \emdash in fact, in the \'etale and fppf
  1306	topologies as well.  Therefore, the absolute Picard functor $\Pic_X$ is never
  1307	representable.  So, in the hope of obtaining a representable functor
  1308	that differs as little as possible from $\Pic_X$, we now define a
  1309	sequence of three successively more promising relative functors.
  1310	
  1311	\begin{dfn}\label{df:Pfs}
  1312	  The {\it relative Picard functor} $\Pic_{X/S}$ is defined by
  1313		$$\Pic_{X/S}(T):=\Pic(X_T)\big/\Pic(T).$$
  1314	 Denote its associated sheaves in the Zariski, \'etale, and fppf
  1315	topologies  by
  1316		$$\Pic_{(X/S)\zar},\ \Pic_{(X/S)\et},\
  1317		\Pic_{(X/S)\fppf}.$$
  1318	 \end{dfn}
  1319	
  1320	We now have a sequence of five Picard functors, and each one maps
  1321	naturally into the next.  So each one maps naturally into any of its
  1322	successors.  If the latter functor is one of the three just displayed,
  1323	then it is a sheaf in the indicated topology; in fact, it is the sheaf
  1324	associated to any one of its predecessors, and the map between them is
  1325	the natural map from a presheaf to its associated sheaf, as is easy to
  1326	check.  In particular, the three displayed sheaves are the sheaves
  1327	associated to the absolute Picard functor $\Pic_X$, as well as to the
  1328	relative Picard functor $\Pic_{X/S}$.
  1329	
  1330	Since $\Pic_{X/S}$ is not a priori a sheaf, it is remarkable that it is
  1331	representable so often in practice.
  1332	
  1333	Note that, for every $S$-scheme $T$, each $T$-point of
  1334	$\Pic_{(X/S)\fppf}$, or element of $\Pic_{(X/S)\fpqc}(T)$, is
  1335	represented by an invertible sheaf $\mc L'$ on $X_{T'}$ for some
  1336	fppf-covering $T'\to T$.    Moreover, there must
  1337	be an fppf-covering $T''\to T'\x_T T'$ such that the two pullbacks of
  1338	$\mc L'$ to $X_{T''}$ are isomorphic \emdash or to put it informally, the
  1339	restrictions of $\mc L'$ must agree on a covering of the overlaps.
  1340	
  1341	Furthermore, a second such sheaf $\mc L_1$ on $X_{T_1}$ represents the
  1342	same $T$-point if and only if there is an fppf-covering $T_1'\to T_1\x_T
  1343	T'$ such that the pullbacks of $\mc L'$ and $\mc L_1$ to $X_{T_1'}$ are
  1344	isomorphic.  Technically, this condition includes the preceding one,
  1345	which concerns the case where $T_1=T'$ and $\mc L_1=\mc L'$ since $\mc
  1346	L'$ must represent the same $T$-point as itself.  Of course, similar
  1347	considerations apply to the Picard functors for the Zariski and \'etale
  1348	topologies as well.

  1377	The main result of this section is the following comparison theorem.
  1378	It identifies two useful conditions: the first guarantees that the first
  1379	three relative functors can be viewed as subfunctors of the fourth;
  1380	together, the two conditions guarantee that all four functors coincide.
  1381	The second condition has three successively weaker forms.  Before we can
  1382	prove the theorem, we must develop some theory.

  1387	f_{\smash{T}*}\mc O_{\!X_T}$.

\section*{3 \quad The symmetric powers of a curve}

Both in order to understand the structure of the Jacobian, and as an aid in
its construction, we shall need to study the symmetric powers of $C$.

For any variety $V$, the symmetric group $S_r$ on $r$ letters acts on the
product of $r$ copies $V^r$ of $V$ by permuting the factors, and we want to
define the $r$th symmetric power $V^{(r)}$ of $V$ to be the quotient
$S_r \backslash V^r$. The next proposition demonstrates the existence of
$V^{(r)}$ and lists its main properties.

A morphism $\varphi \colon V^r \to T$ is said to be \textit{symmetric} if
$\varphi\sigma = \varphi$ for all $\sigma$ in $S_r$.

\paragraph{Proposition 3.1.}
\textit{Let $V$ be a variety over $k$. Then there exists a variety $V^{(r)}$
and a symmetric morphism $\pi \colon V^r \to V^{(r)}$ having the following
properties:}

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \textit{as a topological space, $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ is the quotient
of $V^r$ by $S_r$;}
\item[(b)] \textit{for any open affine subset $U$ of $V$, $U^{(r)}$ is an
open affine subset of $V^{(r)}$ and}
\[
  \Gamma(U^{(r)}, \mathcal{O}_{V^{(r)}})
  = \Gamma(U^r, \mathcal{O}_{V^r})^{S_r}
\]
\textit{(set of elements fixed by the action of $S_r$).}
\end{enumerate}

\textit{The pair $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ has the following universal property:
every symmetric $k$-morphism $\varphi \colon V^r \to T$ factors uniquely
through $\pi$.}

\textit{The map $\pi$ is finite, surjective, and separable.}

\paragraph{Proof.}
If $V$ is affine, say $V = \operatorname{Specm}(A)$, define $V^{(r)}$ to be
$\operatorname{Specm}((A \otimes_k \cdots \otimes_k A)^{S_r})$. In the
general case, write $V$ as a union $\bigcup U_i$ of open affines, and construct
% [sic: printed "construct V"; the context requires "construct V^{(r)}".]
$V$ by patching together the $U_i^{(r)}$. See Mumford 1970, II, \S 7, p66,
and III, \S 11, p112, for the details. \hfill $\square$

The pair $(V^{(r)}, \pi)$ is uniquely determined up to a unique isomorphism
by its universal property. It is called the $r$th \textit{symmetric power} of
$V$.

\paragraph{Proposition 3.2.}
\textit{The symmetric power $C^{(r)}$ of a nonsingular curve is nonsingular.}

\paragraph{Proof.}
We may assume that $k$ is algebraically closed. The most likely candidate for
a singular point on $C^{(r)}$ is the image $Q$ of a fixed point
$(P, \ldots, P)$ of $S_r$ on $C^r$, where $P$ is a closed point of $C$. The
completion $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_P$ of the local ring at $P$ is isomorphic to
$k[[X]]$, and so
\[
  \widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{(P,\ldots,P)}
  \approx k[[X]] \widehat{\otimes} \cdots \widehat{\otimes} k[[X]]
  \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]].
\]
It follows that
$\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_Q \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]^{S_r}$, where $S_r$
acts by permuting the variables. The fundamental theorem on symmetric
functions says that, over any ring, a symmetric polynomial can be expressed
as a polynomial in the elementary symmetric functions
$\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r$. This implies that
\[
  k[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]^{S_r} = k[[\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r]],
\]
which is regular, and so $Q$ is nonsingular.

For a general point $Q = \pi(P, P, \ldots, P', \ldots)$ with $P$ occurring
$r'$ times, $P'$ occurring $r''$ times, and so on,
\[
  \widehat{\mathcal{O}}_Q
  \approx k[[X_1, \ldots, X_{r'}]]^{S_{r'}} \widehat{\otimes}
  k[[X_1, \ldots, X_{r''}]]^{S_{r''}} \widehat{\otimes} \cdots,
\]
which the same argument shows to be regular. \hfill $\square$

\section*{5 \quad The canonical maps from the symmetric powers of $C$ to its
Jacobian variety}

Throughout this section $C$ will be a complete nonsingular curve of genus
$g > 0$. Assume there is a $k$-rational point $P$ on $C$, and write $f$ for
the map $f^P$ defined in \S 2.

Let $f^r$ be the map $C^r \to J$ sending $(P_1, \dots, P_r)$ to
$f(P_1) + \dots + f(P_r)$. On points, $f^r$ is the map
$(P_1, \dots, P_r) \mapsto [P_1 + \dots + P_r - rP]$. Clearly it is
symmetric, and so induces a map $f^{(r)} \colon C^{(r)} \to J$. We can regard
$f^{(r)}$ as being the map sending an effective divisor $D$ of degree $r$ on
$C$ to the linear equivalence class of $D - rP$. The fibre of the map
$f^{(r)} \colon C^{(r)}(k) \to J(k)$ containing $D$ can be identified with the
space of effective divisors linearly equivalent to $D$, that is, with the
linear system $|D|$. The image of $C^{(r)}$ in $J$ is a closed subvariety
$W^r$ of $J$, which can also be written $W^r = f(C) + \dots + f(C)$ ($r$
summands).

\paragraph{Theorem 5.1.}
\textit{(a) For all $r \le g$, the morphism $f^{(r)} \colon C^{(r)} \to W^r$
is birational; in particular, $f^{(g)}$ is a birational map from $C^{(g)}$
onto $J$.}

\textit{(b) Let $D$ be an effective divisor of degree $r$ on $C$, and let $F$
be the fibre of $f^{(r)}$ containing $D$. Then no tangent vector to $C^{(r)}$
at $D$ maps to zero under $(df^{(r)})_D$ unless it lies in the direction of
$F$; in other words, the sequence}
\[
  0 \to T_D(F) \to T_D(C^{(r)}) \to T_a(J), \quad a = f^{(r)}(D),
\]
\textit{is exact. In particular,
$(df^{(r)})_D \colon T_D(C^{(r)}) \to T_a(J)$ is injective if $|D|$ has
dimension zero.}

The proof will occupy the rest of this section.

For $D$ a divisor on $C$, we write $h^0(D)$ for the dimension of
\[
  H^0(C, \mathcal{L}(D)) = \{ f \in k(C) \mid (f) + D \ge 0 \}
\]
and $h^1(D)$ for the dimension of $H^1(C, \mathcal{L}(D))$. Recall that
\[
  h^0(D) - h^1(D) = \deg(D) + 1 - g,
\]
and that $H^1(C, \mathcal{L}(D))^{\vee} = H^0(C, \Omega^1(-D))$, which can be
identified with the set of $\omega \in \Omega^1_{k(C)/k}$ whose divisor
$(\omega) \ge D$.

\paragraph{Lemma 5.2.}
\textit{(a) Let $D$ be a divisor on $C$ such that $h^1(D) > 0$; then there is
a nonempty open subset $U$ of $C$ such that $h^1(D + Q) = h^1(D) - 1$ for all
points $Q$ in $U$, and $h^1(D + Q) = h^1(D)$ for $Q \notin U$.}

\textit{(b) For any $r \le g$, there is an open subset $U$ of $C^r$ such that
$h^0(\sum P_i) = 1$ for all $(P_1, \dots, P_r)$ in $U$.}

\paragraph{Corollary 5.5.}
\textit{For all $r \le g$, $f^r \colon C^r \to W^r$ has degree $r!$.}

\paragraph{Proof.}

\paragraph{Remark 5.6.}
(a) The theorem shows that $J$ is the unique abelian variety birationally
equivalent to $C^{(g)}$. This observation is the basis of Weil's construction
of the Jacobian. (See \S 7.)

(b) The exact sequence in (5.1b) can be regarded as a geometric statement of
the Riemann-Roch theorem (see especially the end of the proof). In fact it is
possible to prove the Riemann-Roch theorem this way (see Mattuck and Mayer
1963).

(c) As we observed above, the fibre of
$f^{(r)} \colon C^{(r)}(k) \to J(k)$ containing $D$ can be identified with
the linear system $|D|$. More precisely, the fibre of the map of functors
$C^{(r)} \to J$ is the functor $\Div_C^D$ of (3.14); therefore the fibre of
$f^{(r)}$ containing $D$ (in the sense of algebraic spaces) is a copy of
projective space of dimension $h^0(D) - 1$. Corollary 3.10 of Chapter I shows
that conversely every copy of projective space in $C^{(r)}$ is contained in
some fibre of $f^{(r)}$. Consequently, the closed points of the Jacobian can
be identified with the set of maximal subvarieties of $C^{(r)}$ isomorphic to
projective space.

Note that for $r > 2g - 2$, $|D|$ has dimension $r - g$, and so
$(df^{(r)})_D$ is surjective, for all $D$. Therefore $f^{(r)}$ is smooth (see
Hartshorne 1977, III 10.4), and the fibres of $f^{(r)}$ are precisely the
copies of $\mathbb{P}^{r-g}$ contained in $C^{(r)}$. This last observation is
the starting point of Chow's construction of the Jacobian Chow 1954.

   708	Below will construct the {\v C}ech-to-cohomology spectral sequence, see

   710	A special case of that spectral sequence is the Mayer-Vietoris
   711	long exact sequence. Since it is such a basic, useful and easy to understand
   712	variant of the spectral sequence we treat it here separately.

   714	\begin{lemma}
   715	\label{lemma-injective-restriction-surjective}
   716	\begin{slogan}
   717	Injectives are flasque.
   718	\end{slogan}
   719	Let $X$ be a ringed space.
   720	Let $U' \subset U \subset X$ be open subspaces.
   721	For any injective $\mathcal{O}_X$-module $\mathcal{I}$ the
   722	restriction mapping
   723	$\mathcal{I}(U) \to \mathcal{I}(U')$ is surjective.
   724	\end{lemma}

   726	\begin{proof}
   727	Let $j : U \to X$ and $j' : U' \to X$ be the open immersions.
   728	Recall that $j_!\mathcal{O}_U$ is the extension by zero of
   729	$\mathcal{O}_U = \mathcal{O}_X|_U$, see
   730	Sheaves, Section \ref{sheaves-section-open-immersions}.
   731	Since $j_!$ is a left adjoint to restriction we see that
   732	for any sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ of $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules
   733	$$
   734	\Hom_{\mathcal{O}_X}(j_!\mathcal{O}_U, \mathcal{F})
   735	=
   736	\Hom_{\mathcal{O}_U}(\mathcal{O}_U, \mathcal{F}|_U)
   737	=
   738	\mathcal{F}(U)
   739	$$

   745	$$
   746	j'_!\mathcal{O}_{U'} \longrightarrow j_!\mathcal{O}_U

"""Parse leanblueprint ``.tex`` and Lean sources into the graph.

The blueprint and the Lean files are the *reference* for the mathematical
content and its structure; the graph adds the layer they cannot hold (status,
provenance, comments, failed attempts). ``sync`` is a one-way reconcile:

* **Two independent node populations.** A blueprint item is keyed by its LaTeX
  ``\\label``; a Lean declaration is keyed by its fully-qualified name. There is
  no 1-to-1 correspondence — ``\\lean{...}`` links them with a *many-to-many*
  ``formalizes`` edge. Both ids are ``sha1("<kind>:<key>")[:12]`` so they are
  uniform and opaque; the human-readable surface is the blueprint / Lean / UI.

* **Owned vs authored.** ``sync`` only ever writes the fields it owns (title,
  content_type, body, the derived ``lean_status``) and the edges it generated
  (tagged ``generated:``). Everything a human or agent added
  — ``origin`` / source, ``tags``, ``status``, comments, hand-drawn edges — is
  left untouched. Re-running ``sync`` is idempotent.

* **No silent deletes.** A node whose source key vanished is marked
  ``stale: true`` (keeping its comments and metadata), never removed.

The edge endpoints are *deterministic*: ``\\lean{Gauss.IsEven}`` seeds exactly
the string the Lean node is keyed on, so ``sync`` needs no cross-reference index.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

from .graph import Graph, HGraphError, node_id


def load_config(root: str | Path) -> dict:
    """Read ``<root>/hgraph/config.yaml`` if present, so a bare ``sync`` (or
    ``dashboard``/``site``) knows where things are. Recognised keys (paths are
    relative to ``<root>``)::

        blueprint: blueprint/blueprint.tex
        lean: [Lean]                 # a path or a list of paths
        site:                        # optional — see hgraph.site's docstring
          title: ...
          subtitle: ...
          overview: overview.md
          repo: owner/name
          accent: '#B4530B'          # this project's colour (or a full theme:);
                                      # applies to its card + blueprint view
          tabs:                      # extra content tabs on its blueprint view
            - {id: people, label: People, content: people.md}

    Returns ``{"blueprint": <abs path or None>, "lean": [<abs path>, ...],
    "site": <the site: block, verbatim, or {}>}``.
    """
    root = Path(root)
    p = root / "hgraph" / "config.yaml"
    if not p.exists():
        return {"blueprint": None, "lean": [], "site": {}}
    data = yaml.safe_load(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) or {}
    bp = data.get("blueprint")
    lean = data.get("lean") or []
    if isinstance(lean, str):
        lean = [lean]
    return {
        "blueprint": str(root / bp) if bp else None,
        "lean": [str(root / l) for l in lean],
        "site": data.get("site") or {},
    }

def _first_arg(macro: str, text: str) -> str | None:
    """The raw (un-split) argument of the first ``\\macro{…}`` — for markers whose
    argument is a single value that may contain commas (``\\source{Lee, p. 42}``)."""
    m = re.search(r"\\" + macro + r"\{(.*?)\}", text, re.DOTALL)
    return m.group(1).strip() if m else None


def _statement_fields(env: str, title, inner: str) -> dict:
    # a \label inside display math names an equation, not the statement
    labels = _macro_args("label", _MATH_SPAN_RE.sub("", inner))
    body = _strip_macros(inner)
    title, body = _lift_title(title, body)
    return {
        "label": labels[0] if labels else None,
        # a statement may carry more than one \label (e.g. a new semantic label
        # plus the original book's legacy label, kept so old \ref{}/\uses{} calls
        # still resolve) — every one of them must point back to this same node.
        "labels": labels,
        "title": (title or (labels[0] if labels else env)).strip(),
        "content_type": THM_ENVS[env],
        "lean": _macro_args("lean", inner),
        "uses": _macro_args("uses", inner),
        "leanok": bool(re.search(r"\\leanok\b", inner)),
        "mathlibok": bool(re.search(r"\\mathlibok\b", inner)),

        # omitted routine verification). Not a status to be fixed by syncing —
        # an author's statement about the maths, surfaced to the reader as-is.

def _upsert(g: Graph, nid: str, *, title: str, type: str, content: str,
            owned: dict, dry_run: bool = False) -> bool:
    """Create the node, or overwrite exactly the owned fields — leaving every
    authored field (origin, tags, status, …) in place, clearing ``stale``, and
    unsetting any owned field that is now empty (e.g. a doc comment removed).

    Return whether the graph differs from the requested state.  ``dry_run``
    performs the same comparison without writing, which lets ``serve`` detect
    pending sync work using the reconciliation rules themselves.
    """
    clean = {k: v for k, v in owned.items() if v is not None}
    empty = [k for k, v in owned.items() if v is None]
    if g.has_node(nid):
        n = g.get_node(nid)
        changed = n.title != title or n.type != type or n.content != content
        changed |= any(n.meta.get(k) != v for k, v in clean.items())
        changed |= any(k in n.meta for k in ("stale", *empty))
        if changed and not dry_run:
            g.modify_node(nid, title=title, type=type, content=content,
                          set_meta=clean, unset=["stale", *empty])
    else:
        changed = True
        if not dry_run:
            g.add_node(title, type=type, id=nid, content=content, **clean)
    return changed
